demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette: Samantha, a 46-year-old forensic analyst of Oceania descent, has been struggling with the aftermath of an unexpected and traumatic death in her life. Her husband’s sudden passing left her feeling overwhelmed and lost, experiences that have significantly impacted how she navigates her daily routine. Since his death, Samantha finds herself frequently avoiding work. She sees no point in going through the motions anymore because nothing seems meaningful to her. This avoidance is a direct result of her profound sense of loss and disillusionment. As she had come to believe that her life has been utterly destroyed by this trauma, she struggles to find any significance in her daily tasks or professional responsibilities. The memory of what happened continues to haunt Samantha. She often hears snippets of conversations from the time surrounding his death, auditory cues that bring her back to a moment frozen in time—a snapshot in her mind. The overwhelming emotions that accompany these memories make it difficult for her to function normally. When she is overwhelmed by these recollections, she has to stop whatever she is doing and take a moment to process the intense feelings. Samantha’s coping mechanisms have also become maladaptive. She delays sleep until very late, often staying up all night as a way of managing her anxiety and distress. This undereating and lack of sleep further exacerbate her emotional state, making it harder for her to deal with the memories that flood her mind at unexpected moments. These maladaptive strategies have a reciprocal effect on Samantha’s memory. Her tendency to avoid work and restrict food intake has led to periods of intense focus on past events, which are then replayed in her mind as vivid snapshots. The more she avoids dealing with her emotions head-on, the more overwhelming these memories become. This cycle only reinforces her negative appraisals that life is devoid of meaning and that her faith in people and a higher power has been shattered. What frightens Samantha most is the thought of losing control and being unable to manage her intense feelings on her own. She fears that her work performance will suffer even more, straining her relationships with colleagues who have noticed her declining engagement at the office. Her maladaptive behaviors have already begun to take a toll on her professional life. Despite these challenges, Samantha recognizes the need for help and is seeking therapy in hopes of finding meaning again. She wants to regain control over her life and find ways to cope more effectively without feeling overwhelmed by her memories. As she begins this journey, her greatest hope is to rebuild some semblance of a fulfilling existence beyond the trauma that has so profoundly altered her worldview.
